{{Short description|Mathematical conjecture}}
{{unsolved|mathematics|What is the upper bound for the number of squares in finite arithmetic progressions?}}
'''Rudin's conjecture''' is a mathematical conjecture in [[additive combinatorics]] and [[elementary number theory]] about an upper bound for the number of squares in finite [[arithmetic progression]]s. The conjecture, which has applications in the theory of [[trigonometric series]], was first stated by [[Walter Rudin]] in his 1960 paper ''Trigonometric series with gaps''.<ref>{{cite book|editor=Granville, Andrew|editor2=Nathanson, Melvyn Bernard|editor3=Solymosi, József|editor3-link= József Solymosi |author=Cilleruelo, Javier|author2=Granville, Andrew|chapter=Lattice points on circles, squares in arithmetic progressions and sumsets of squares|title=Additive combinatorics|year=2007|series=CRM Proceedings & Lecture Notes, vol. 43|publisher=American Mathematical Society|pages=241–262|isbn=978-0-8218-7039-6 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9q6_O6AwAhQC&pg=PA241}} [https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0608109 arXiv.org preprint]</ref><ref>{{cite journal|jstor=24900534|author=Rudin, Walter|title=Trigonometric series with gaps|journal=Journal of Mathematics and Mechanics|year=1960|volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=203–227}}</ref><ref name=LMS>{{cite journal|journal=LMS Journal of Computation and Mathematics|volume=17|issue=1|year=2014|pages=58–76|title=On a conjecture of Rudin on squares in arithmetic progressions|author=González-Jiménez, Enrique|author2=Xarles, Xavier|doi=10.1112/S1461157013000259|arxiv=1301.5122}}</ref>

For positive integers <math>N, q, a</math> define the expression <math>Q(N; q, a)</math> to be the number of [[square number|perfect square]]s in the arithmetic progression <math>qn + a</math>, for <math>n = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1</math>, and define <math>Q(N)</math> to be the maximum of the set {{math|{''Q''(''N''; ''q'', ''a'') : ''q'', ''a'' ≥ 1} }}. The conjecture asserts (in [[big O notation]]) that <math>Q(N) = O(\sqrt { N })</math> and in its stronger form that, if <math>N > 6</math>, <math>Q(N) = Q(N; 24, 1)</math>.<ref name=LMS/> This progression begins with <math>1, 25, 49, 73, 97, 121, ...</math> and its square terms correspond to indices that are generalized [[pentagonal number]]s. For <math>N = 5</math>, the arithmetic progression <math>120n + 49</math> contains four squares <math>(49, 169, 289, 529)</math>, so <math>Q(5)=4</math>, whereas <math>24n+1</math> only contains three squares in its first five terms.

==Background and partial results==
The problem of finding squares in arithmetic progressions is famously connected to [[Fermat]], who proved that no four squares can be in a non-constant arithmetic progression. This result is equivalent to stating that <math>Q(4) = 3</math>. The general question of bounding the number of squares led to a conjecture by [[Paul Erdős]] that for any arithmetic progression of length <math>N</math>, the number of squares must be <math>o(N)</math> ([[little-o notation]]). This was proven by [[Endre Szemerédi]] as a consequence of [[Szemerédi's theorem]] on arithmetic progressions.<ref name=LMS/>

Following Szemerédi's result, the upper bound for <math>Q(N)</math> was progressively improved. Bombieri, Granville, and Pintz established a bound of <math>O\!\left(N^{\tfrac{2}{3}+o(1)}\right)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal 
 | last1 = Bombieri 
 | first1 = Enrico 
 | last2 = Granville 
 | first2 = Andrew 
 | last3 = Pintz 
 | first3 = János 
 | title = Squares in arithmetic progressions 
 | journal = Duke Mathematical Journal 
 | volume = 66 
 | issue = 3 
 | pages = 369–385 
 | year = 1992 
 | doi = 10.1215/S0012-7094-92-06612-9
}}</ref> This was later refined by Bombieri and Zannier to <math>O\!\left(N^{\tfrac{3}{5}+o(1)}\right)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal 
 | last1 = Bombieri 
 | first1 = Enrico 
 | last2 = Zannier 
 | first2 = Umberto 
 | title = A note on squares in arithmetic progressions. II 
 | journal = Rendiconti Lincei - Matematica e Applicazioni 
 | volume = 13 
 | issue = 2 
 | pages = 69–75 
 | year = 2002 
 | mr = 1949479
 | url = http://www.bdim.eu/item?fmt=pdf&id=RLIN_2002_9_13_2_69_0
}}</ref>

Enrique Gonzalez-Jimenez and Xavier Xarles verified in 2014 that the Strong Rudin's Conjecture holds for all <math>6 \le N \le 52</math>. Based on this evidence, they proposed a "''Super-Strong Rudin's Conjecture''", which states that for specific values of <math>N</math> where <math>Q(N)</math> is expected to increase (specifically when <math>N = GP_k + 1 \ge 8</math>, where <math>GP_k</math> is the <math>k</math>-th generalized pentagonal number), the arithmetic progression <math>24n+1</math> is the only one, up to equivalence, that achieves the maximum number of squares.<ref name=LMS/>
